japan-line-datenleck-china.json.name_en: Japan: LINE Data Breach — 86 Million Users' Data Accessible in China
japan-line-datenleck-china.json.description_en: Japan's most-used messaging app LINE (86 million users) granted a Chinese subcontractor access to personal data of Japanese users, including names, phone numbers, and chat content. The incident triggered a national debate on data sovereignty and dependence on foreign technology companies. The Japanese government and numerous municipalities suspended their use of LINE for public services.
actors_en: Japanese Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC)

timeline_en.title_en: LINE as quasi-public infrastructure
timeline_en.description_en: LINE becomes Japan's dominant communication platform with 86 million users — more than two thirds of the population. Hundreds of municipal administrations use LINE for citizen services, COVID-19 surveys, and official communication. LINE develops parts of its software in China through Naver subsidiaries.

timeline_en.title_en: Chinese engineers' access to Japanese user data exposed
timeline_en.description_en: Asahi Shimbun reveals that Chinese employees of LINE subcontractors could access personal data of Japanese users, including names, phone numbers, and chat histories. At least 32 accesses to Japanese user data are documented. LINE had previously claimed that all data was stored in Japan.

timeline_en.title_en: Government and municipalities halt LINE use
timeline_en.description_en: The Japanese Ministry of Internal Affairs orders a review. Numerous municipal administrations halt their use of LINE for citizen services. The My Number national ID service is decoupled from LINE. LINE's CEO publicly apologizes and promises full data migration back to Japan.

timeline_en.title_en: Renewed data breach scandal and regulatory debate
timeline_en.description_en: Another incident in 2023 shows that data of 440,000 LINE users was again compromised via the Naver Cloud. The Japanese government intensifies calls for 'data localization' and the separation of LINE's infrastructure from its South Korean parent Naver. The case advances Japan's data protection legislation.

sources_titles_en: Japan to probe Line over user data accessible from China

jemen-drohnenkrieg-ki.json.name_en: Yemen: AI-Assisted Drone Strikes with High Civilian Casualty Rates
jemen-drohnenkrieg-ki.json.description_en: US and Saudi forces have deployed AI-assisted targeting systems for drone strikes in Yemen. The US has conducted drone strikes since 2009; since 2015 the Saudi-led coalition has added airstrikes. Organizations such as Mwatana for Human Rights and Airwars document persistently high civilian casualty figures, partly traced to flawed algorithmic targeting. UN experts criticize inadequate proportionality reviews.

timeline_en.title_en: First US drone strikes in Yemen
timeline_en.description_en: The US begins covert drone strikes in Yemen under the heading 'Counterterrorism Operations.' Targeting systems use metadata analysis and signals intelligence. The first documented strike in al-Ma'jalah kills at least 41 civilians, including 14 women and 21 children.

timeline_en.title_en: Saudi coalition escalates — US targeting data flows in
timeline_en.description_en: With the start of the Saudi military intervention, the US supplies target coordinates and logistical support. Algorithmic analysis of phone metadata and movement patterns is used to identify suspects. This led to entire family groups being classified as 'combatants.'

timeline_en.title_en: Mwatana documents 510 unlawful strikes
timeline_en.description_en: The Yemeni human rights organization Mwatana for Human Rights publishes a report documenting 510 potentially unlawful coalition airstrikes since 2015, including attacks on weddings, schools, and clinics. Pattern-recognition algorithms tracking vehicle clusters led to misclassifications.

timeline_en.title_en: UN expert panel criticizes targeting algorithms
timeline_en.description_en: The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen criticizes in its annual report the lack of transparency in algorithmic targeting on both sides. Compensation for civilian victims' families is not forthcoming. International calls for an AI weapons halt in the Yemen conflict grow but remain without consequence.

sources_titles_en: Day of Judgment: The Role of the United States in Civilian Harm in Yemen

jordanien-pegasus-journalisten.json.name_en: Jordan: Pegasus Spyware Against Journalists, Lawyers, and Civil Society
jordanien-pegasus-journalisten.json.description_en: Jordan deployed the Pegasus spyware made by Israel's NSO Group to surveil journalists, lawyers, human rights defenders, and activists. A joint 2022 report by Citizen Lab and Front Line Defenders identified at least 35 victims in Jordan. Access Now confirmed additional cases in 2023. Pegasus enables full compromise of mobile devices without user interaction (zero-click attacks): microphone, camera, messages, and passwords are covertly exfiltrated. The cases show a pattern of targeted suppression of critical voices.

timeline_en.title_en: First documented targeting operations in Jordan
timeline_en.description_en: Citizen Lab finds initial traces of Pegasus infrastructure affecting Jordanian civilians. Jordan is considered a close ally of Western states and obtains access to Pegasus licensing through NSO Group. Those affected include journalists reporting on issues such as economic corruption and political opposition, as well as lawyers representing politically persecuted clients.

timeline_en.title_en: Citizen Lab and Front Line Defenders reveal 35 victims
timeline_en.description_en: A joint report by Citizen Lab and Front Line Defenders publishes forensic evidence of Pegasus infections on devices of 35 journalists, human rights defenders, and lawyers in Jordan. Among them are staff of leading news outlets and members of the Jordanian Bar Association. NSO Group denies misuse; Jordan does not respond.

timeline_en.title_en: Further revelations: lawyers and union leaders affected
timeline_en.description_en: Additional forensic analyses show that the head of the Jordanian Bar Association and union representatives were also surveilled with Pegasus. The attacks used zero-click exploits that require no interaction from the victim and leave no visible trace. The surveillance pattern points to coordinated state use against people organizing legal challenges or political opposition.

timeline_en.title_en: Access Now confirms further victims — no accountability
timeline_en.description_en: Access Now publishes reports in 2023 confirming further Jordanian Pegasus victims, including women's rights activists and media workers. Jordan faces international pressure to open investigations but does not respond. NSO Group says it sells only to vetted government customers. No judicial or parliamentary review takes place in Jordan. The cases become part of the global debate on regulating commercial spyware.

sources_titles_en: Front Line Defenders: Jordan — Human Rights Defenders Under Surveillance

kambodscha-chinesische-scam-compounds.js.name_en: Cambodia: Chinese Scam Compounds with AI and Human Trafficking
kambodscha-chinesische-scam-compounds.js.description_en: In Sihanoukville and other locations in Cambodia, Chinese criminal organizations operate large-scale scam compounds where forced labor by trafficking victims is combined with AI tools. The UN estimates that over 100,000 people are held in such facilities across Southeast Asia. AI-assisted chatbots, deepfakes, and automated social engineering systems are used to deceive scam victims worldwide. Cambodian authorities profit from corruption and partly look the other way.
affectedRights_en: prohibition of slavery and forced labor

timeline_en.title_en: Emergence of scam compounds in Sihanoukville
timeline_en.description_en: Chinese investors looking for alternatives after the closure of gambling venues in Macau and China build large-scale operations in Sihanoukville and the Dara Sakor Special Economic Zone. Initially disguised as online gambling hubs, the compounds are increasingly repurposed for cyber fraud. The facilities evolve into guarded complexes that workers cannot escape.

timeline_en.title_en: UN report exposes scale of trafficking
timeline_en.description_en: The UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) publishes a report estimating that over 100,000 people are working under coercion in scam compounds across Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos, and Thailand. Many were lured to the region with false job offers. Al Jazeera and ProPublica report on victims forced to run romance scams and crypto-investment fraud, accompanied by physical punishment for missing targets.

timeline_en.title_en: AI integration into scam systems scales the harm
timeline_en.description_en: Investigations show the compounds increasingly deploy AI tools, including deepfake software for video calls (to make scammers appear younger, more attractive, or as a different gender), automated chatbots based on ChatGPT for first contact, and AI-assisted translation for multilingual scam campaigns. Victims in over 100 countries are harmed, with total damages in the billions.

timeline_en.title_en: International pressure and partial clearances
timeline_en.description_en: Under international pressure, Cambodia conducts some raids without achieving structural change. China pressures Cambodian authorities to repatriate its citizens. The US imposes sanctions on Cambodian officials linked to the compounds. UNODC and victims' rights groups call for a regional approach as many compounds migrate to Myanmar and Laos.

sources_titles_en: Online Scam Operations and Trafficking into Forced Criminality in Southeast Asia
Hundreds of thousands trafficked into online criminality across SE Asia
China's Exploitation of Scam Centers in Southeast Asia
Scam States: The Cybercrime-Corruption Complex in Southeast Asia

kambodscha-internet-gateway.json.name_en: Cambodia: National Internet Gateway for State Control of All Data Traffic
kambodscha-internet-gateway.json.description_en: The Cambodian government issued a 2021 decree establishing a National Internet Gateway (NIG) intended to route all the country's internet traffic through a centrally state-controlled infrastructure. The system enables real-time surveillance, targeted censorship of specific websites and services, and identification of users. Critics see it as adoption of China's 'Great Firewall' model. According to Access Now and Human Rights Watch, the measure is directed against the political opposition, independent media, and civil society organizations.

timeline_en.title_en: Royal government issues NIG decree
timeline_en.description_en: The Cambodian government passes Sub-Decree No. 23 establishing a National Internet Gateway. The document requires all internet service providers to route their traffic through the state gateway. Technically the system is comparable to China's 'Great Firewall' approach. International organizations and tech companies immediately warn of serious consequences for freedom of expression and data security.

timeline_en.title_en: Implementation plans and negotiations with ISPs
timeline_en.description_en: The government begins compelling internet service providers to implement the technical rerouting. Human Rights Watch documents threats against ISPs that voice concerns. The government insists the gateway serves only 'cybersecurity' and tax control purposes. Civil society organizations in Cambodia report growing pressure on activists and journalists.

timeline_en.title_en: Partial launch — first documented blocks
timeline_en.description_en: VOA Khmer and local observers report a first partial activation of the gateway. Selected news and opposition websites are targeted for blocking. The government blocks several critical media platforms shortly before the 2023 parliamentary elections. Access Now documents an increasing pattern of internet shutdowns as a tool of state control around political events.

timeline_en.title_en: Widespread self-censorship — international condemnation without effect
timeline_en.description_en: The prospect of full NIG implementation leads to widespread self-censorship among Cambodian journalists and civil society. Human Rights Watch and Access Now call on the international community to take concrete action. Independent media relocate their editorial offices abroad. The government of Hun Manet (son of the long-time ruler) continues the course despite international criticism.

sources_titles_en: Cambodia's National Internet Gateway: A tool for censorship and surveillance
Cambodia Internet Gateway reporting

kanada-ki-wohlfahrt-ontario.json.name_en: Canada Ontario: Algorithmic Cuts to Social Assistance
kanada-ki-wohlfahrt-ontario.json.description_en: Since 2014, the province of Ontario has used an algorithmic system that automatically decides on social assistance applications and imposes benefit cuts. The system, based on a scoring model, prioritizes and filters applications without human review. Vulnerable populations — especially Indigenous people, people with disabilities, and single parents — are disproportionately affected by the cuts.
actors_en: Ontario Ministry of Community and Social Services

timeline_en.title_en: SAMS system replaces manual processing
timeline_en.description_en: Ontario introduces the Social Assistance Management System (SAMS), which automates processing of Ontario Works and the Ontario Disability Support Program. The system, built on Curam Software (IBM), replaces a 20-year-old system. From day one, complaints about erroneous benefit cuts pile up.

timeline_en.title_en: Mass miscalculations and cuts
timeline_en.description_en: The Ontario Ombudsman receives hundreds of complaints. Social assistance recipients report that their benefits are cut or suspended without explanation. The system proves error-prone in complex cases — exactly the most vulnerable recipients who need multiple support benefits.

timeline_en.title_en: Ombudsman report documents systematic errors
timeline_en.description_en: The Ontario Ombudsman publishes the report 'The SAMS Story.' It documents that the system systematically made flawed decisions for years without effective controls. Particularly affected: people with disabilities whose special needs were not correctly captured by the system.

timeline_en.title_en: Calls for algorithmic accountability
timeline_en.description_en: Canadian civil liberties groups and researchers demand an Algorithmic Impact Assessment for all government decision-making systems. The Canadian federal government introduces the Algorithmic Impact Assessment Tool — one of the first worldwide. Ontario reforms SAMS step by step.

sources_titles_en: Algorithmic Impact Assessment Tool

kanada-rcmp-clearview.json.name_en: Canada: RCMP Secretly Uses Clearview AI and Violates Privacy Law
kanada-rcmp-clearview.json.description_en: Beginning in 2019, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) secretly used Clearview AI for facial recognition without informing the federal privacy authority or conducting a privacy impact assessment. Following an investigation by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPC), it was determined in 2021 that this use violated the Privacy Act. Clearview AI had scraped billions of facial images from the internet without consent.

timeline_en.title_en: RCMP begins covert use of Clearview AI
timeline_en.description_en: The RCMP signs a contract with Clearview AI and uses the system for criminal investigations. Neither parliament nor the privacy authority are informed. Clearview AI operates a database of more than three billion facial images scraped without consent from social media and other websites.

timeline_en.title_en: OPC opens investigation
timeline_en.description_en: After media reports expose Canadian agencies' use of Clearview AI, the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada opens a formal investigation into the RCMP. At the same time, a joint investigation by privacy authorities in several provinces is launched against Clearview AI itself.

timeline_en.title_en: OPC: RCMP use violates privacy law
timeline_en.description_en: The OPC finds that the RCMP's covert use of Clearview AI violated the Privacy Act. Clearview AI is separately declared illegal in Canada and must end its service for Canadian customers. Privacy authorities in several provinces order Clearview to delete the data of Canadian citizens.

timeline_en.title_en: Legislative gaps persist
timeline_en.description_en: Despite the OPC ruling, there are no criminal consequences for the RCMP. Canada is debating reforms to the Privacy Act, which have not yet been passed. Civil liberties groups call for a complete ban on biometric mass capture by government agencies. Several police agencies state they no longer use Clearview AI.

sources_titles_en: Police use of Facial Recognition Technology in Canada and the way forward — RCMP investigation report
Clearview AI ceases offering its facial recognition technology in Canada
RCMP Use of Face Recognition Tool Violated Privacy Law
RCMP denied using facial recognition technology — then said it had been using it for months

kasachstan-ki-protest-shutdown.json.name_en: Kazakhstan: Internet Shutdown and AI Surveillance During the January 2022 Protests
kasachstan-ki-protest-shutdown.json.description_en: During nationwide protests in January 2022, Kazakhstan shut down the internet completely for five days while security forces used lethal force against demonstrators. At least 238 people were killed. After internet access was restored, the regime used Chinese surveillance technology and facial recognition to identify and arrest thousands of protest participants.
actors_en: Kazakh government / KNB (Committee for National Security)

timeline_en.title_en: Mass protests and internet shutdown
timeline_en.description_en: Protests over gas price hikes escalate into nationwide demonstrations against the government. On January 5, the government shuts down the internet entirely — 19 million people lose access. The shutdown prevents coordination of protests and documentation of violence by security forces.

timeline_en.title_en: Shoot-to-kill order: at least 238 dead
timeline_en.description_en: President Tokayev issues a shoot-to-kill order and calls in CSTO troops (led by Russia). In Almaty, demonstrators are fired on without warning. At least 238 people are killed and thousands injured. The internet shutdown prevents evidence of the scale of violence from reaching the outside world.

timeline_en.title_en: Mass arrests via facial recognition
timeline_en.description_en: After the internet is restored, security forces use surveillance footage and facial recognition to retroactively identify protest participants. Over 12,000 people are arrested. Reports of torture and forced confessions accumulate. Almaty's CCTV network is built on Chinese technology (Hikvision/Dahua).

timeline_en.title_en: Impunity and expansion of surveillance
timeline_en.description_en: No security official is criminally prosecuted for the killings. Instead, hundreds of protesters receive prison sentences. The government further expands the digital surveillance infrastructure. Kazakhstan becomes a model case for the use of internet shutdowns and retrospective facial recognition as instruments of repression.

sources_titles_en: Internet disrupted in Kazakhstan amid energy price protests
Freedom on the Net 2023: Kazakhstan

katar-arbeiter-ueberwachung-wm.json.name_en: Qatar: Digital Surveillance of Migrant Workers During the 2022 World Cup
katar-arbeiter-ueberwachung-wm.json.description_en: In the run-up to the 2022 FIFA World Cup, Qatar deployed digital surveillance systems to control more than two million migrant workers from Southeast Asia and Africa. The kafala sponsorship system was reinforced through digital tools: biometric working-time tracking, GPS tracking on construction sites, and phone surveillance. Amnesty International and The Guardian documented systematic wage theft, passport confiscation, and movement restrictions enabled by these technological control mechanisms.

timeline_en.title_en: Mass recruitment and build-up of digital control systems
timeline_en.description_en: Qatar begins the massive build-up of World Cup infrastructure. Hundreds of thousands of migrant workers are recruited. The kafala system ties residency permits to employers. Biometric systems for time tracking and access control on construction sites are introduced. According to Amnesty International, many workers had their passports confiscated.

timeline_en.title_en: Amnesty reports document systematic exploitation
timeline_en.description_en: Amnesty International publishes comprehensive reports on forced labor, wage theft, and abuse. Digital surveillance systems enable employers to track movements and to report workers who leave construction sites without permission. Heat exposure without adequate protection leads to deaths that are officially undercounted.

timeline_en.title_en: Guardian investigation: over 6,500 dead since 2010
timeline_en.description_en: The Guardian publishes an analysis showing that since the World Cup was awarded in 2010, more than 6,500 migrant workers from five countries (India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka) have died. Digital wage-theft systems and electronic exit bans are documented. Qatar disputes the figures and announces reformed labor protection laws.

timeline_en.title_en: World Cup begins without fundamental system reforms
timeline_en.description_en: The World Cup takes place in November-December 2022. Observers note that despite announced reforms, the kafala system and digital control mechanisms remain largely unchanged. International human rights organizations demand compensation payments from FIFA. FIFA and Qatar agree on a workers' fund that is criticized as insufficient.

sources_titles_en: Qatar's World Cup of Shame

kenia-worldcoin-iris-scan.json.name_en: Kenya: Worldcoin Collects Iris Scans Without Informed Consent
kenia-worldcoin-iris-scan.json.description_en: The company Worldcoin (now: World), co-founded by Sam Altman, launched a global program to capture iris scans as a biometric identifier starting in 2021. In Kenya, thousands of people were recruited with the promise of crypto-token payments without full disclosure regarding the purpose, data storage, and risks. The Kenyan Data Protection Authority and the Interior Ministry suspended its activities in 2023. Investigations in several countries followed.

timeline_en.title_en: Worldcoin launches global iris-scan campaign
timeline_en.description_en: Tools for Humanity builds the so-called 'Orb' — a silver spherical device that captures iris scans and creates a unique 'IrisCode' from them. Scan campaigns are launched in low-income regions worldwide, including Kenya, Ghana, Indonesia, and India. Participants receive WLD crypto tokens as an incentive. Critics object that consent forms are written in unintelligible language and that the consequences of sharing data are not transparently communicated.

timeline_en.title_en: MIT Technology Review exposes problematic practices
timeline_en.description_en: An investigation by MIT Technology Review documents that Worldcoin specifically targets poor populations in developing countries while providing inadequate information about data storage, sharing, and possible risks. In some countries, token promises are not honored. Privacy advocates criticize that biometric raw data — despite the company's claims to the contrary — is temporarily cached on central servers.

timeline_en.title_en: Kenya suspends Worldcoin activities
timeline_en.description_en: The Kenyan Interior Ministry orders the immediate cessation of all Worldcoin operations in the country. The Kenyan Data Protection Authority (ODPC) launches a formal investigation. At the same time, investigations begin in France, Germany, and other European countries. The UK Information Commissioner reviews possible violations of UK GDPR. Worldcoin denies wrongdoing.

timeline_en.title_en: International regulatory wave and corporate rebranding
timeline_en.description_en: After investigations in more than five countries, Worldcoin rebrands itself as 'World' and temporarily suspends operations in several markets. The Kenyan ODPC finds that Worldcoin collected biometric data of Kenyan citizens without an adequate legal basis. Data protection questions about the handling of already collected iris scans remain unresolved. The company nevertheless continues its global expansion.

sources_titles_en: Kenya becomes the first country to suspend Sam Altman's Worldcoin A.I.-crypto scheme
Kenya suspends Worldcoin scans over security, privacy and financial concerns
Worldcoin ignored initial order to stop iris scans in Kenya, records show
What to Know About Worldcoin and the Controversy Around It
Kenya orders Worldcoin to delete biometric data in landmark privacy ruling

kenya-content-moderation.json.description_en: Kenyan workers are employed at poverty wages for the traumatizing annotation of AI training data. The company Sama, on behalf of OpenAI and other tech giants, employs workers who must view and categorize disturbing content such as violence, child abuse, and hate speech for less than two US dollars per hour.

timeline_en.title_en: Sama builds annotation centers in Kenya
timeline_en.description_en: The US company Sama operates data annotation centers in Nairobi, employing Kenyan workers to categorize content. The company markets itself as a social enterprise that fights poverty.

timeline_en.title_en: OpenAI hires Sama for toxicity labeling
timeline_en.description_en: OpenAI contracts Sama to annotate toxic content for training ChatGPT's safety filters. Kenyan workers must read and categorize thousands of texts about sexual abuse, violence, and hate speech to make the AI safer.

timeline_en.title_en: TIME investigation reveals working conditions
timeline_en.description_en: An investigative report by TIME Magazine exposes the traumatizing working conditions at Sama in Nairobi. Workers report psychological harm from constant exposure to disturbing material while earning between $1.32 and $2 per hour.

timeline_en.title_en: Sama terminates OpenAI contract early
timeline_en.description_en: After the TIME investigation is published, Sama ends its contract with OpenAI eight months before the planned conclusion. The company says it intends to withdraw from content moderation.

timeline_en.title_en: International debate over AI labor exploitation
timeline_en.description_en: The revelations spark a broad international debate about the hidden human costs of AI development. Unions and labor rights organizations demand fair pay and psychological support for data annotators in the Global South.

sources_titles_en: The human cost of AI development
Inside the Hidden Battles of Africa's Gig Workers: Content Moderators in Kenya

kolumbien-ki-migration-profiling.json.name_en: Colombia: AI Profiling at the Border Discriminates Against Venezuelan Migrants
kolumbien-ki-migration-profiling.json.description_en: Colombia uses AI-assisted profiling systems at its border with Venezuela, particularly in Cucuta, to screen Venezuelan migrants. The system categorizes migrants by risk profiles based on opaque algorithms that factor in age, place of origin, and travel patterns. Human rights organizations document that the profiling leads to arbitrary rejections and disproportionate surveillance of Venezuelans, even though Colombia is the largest host country for Venezuelan refugees.

timeline_en.title_en: Mass migration from Venezuela and build-up of border control systems
timeline_en.description_en: As the number of Venezuelan migrants in Colombia rises to over 1.8 million, the government invests in digital border infrastructure. With IOM support, biometric systems and databases are built. The Venezuelan migrants' registry (RUMV) is established as the foundation for analytical tools deployed later.

timeline_en.title_en: Introduction of AI-assisted border screening
timeline_en.description_en: Colombian border authorities implement algorithmic risk analysis for arriving Venezuelans. The system uses variables correlated with ethnicity and socioeconomic status. NGOs begin to document patterns of disproportionate rejection and longer questioning of certain migrant groups. Transparency about the algorithms and decision criteria is entirely absent.

timeline_en.title_en: Temporary protection status (TPS) and persistent profiling problems
timeline_en.description_en: Colombia issues Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Venezuelan migrants, an internationally praised instrument. At the same time, human rights organizations report that algorithmic screening at the border continues and that certain groups — especially young men and people from specific Venezuelan regions — are disproportionately classified as 'risk persons.'

timeline_en.title_en: Criticism from human rights organizations and calls for transparency
timeline_en.description_en: Human Rights Watch and local organizations demand transparency about the deployed algorithms and independent oversight of the border system. The Colombian government has not conducted an impact assessment for the AI systems. The profiling system now serves as a model recommended to other Latin American states — a development human rights advocates call alarming.

sources_titles_en: IOM Colombia: Migration Response

kolumbien-ki-protest-ueberwachung.json.description_en: During the 2019-2021 mass protests, Colombian security forces deployed AI-assisted surveillance systems including facial recognition and drones to identify demonstrators. Dozens of activists report targeted threats after participating in protests. Security forces use, among others, Israeli and Chinese surveillance technology.

timeline_en.title_en: Paro Nacional: mass protests begin
timeline_en.description_en: Nationwide protests against the government of President Duque begin. Police deploy a network of more than 20,000 surveillance cameras with facial recognition installed in Bogota in previous years. Drones monitor protest marches.

timeline_en.title_en: 2021 protests: violence and surveillance escalate
timeline_en.description_en: Following the announcement of a tax reform, mass protests erupt again. Security forces respond with brutal violence (at least 80 dead according to NGOs) and intensified digital surveillance. Demonstrators report that they are identified on social media after participating in protests and then threatened.

timeline_en.title_en: Inter-American Commission on Human Rights visits Colombia
timeline_en.description_en: The IACHR documents systematic human rights violations during the protests, including the use of surveillance technology for intimidation. The Commission recommends that Colombia stop using facial recognition during protests.

timeline_en.title_en: New government promises reforms
timeline_en.description_en: The Petro government promises police reform and restrictions on surveillance technology. Civil society organizations such as Fundacion Karisma continue to document the use of facial recognition and demand a legal ban on biometric mass surveillance.

sources_titles_en: #ParoNacionalColombia and Digital Security Considerations for Police Brutality Protests
Paro y pandemia: las respuestas a las protestas masivas en Colombia
Colombia: Represion en la mira
Protestas en Colombia de 2021

kuba-sorm-internet-kontrolle.json.name_en: Cuba: Total Internet Surveillance With Chinese Technology Support
kuba-sorm-internet-kontrolle.json.description_en: Since the gradual introduction of internet access, Cuba has operated a comprehensive surveillance and censorship system combining elements of Russia's SORM system with Chinese network technology. Huawei supplies core infrastructure. The sole state internet provider ETECSA monitors all data traffic. During the #11J protests in 2021, mobile internet was completely shut down. Opposition figures and journalists report targeted surveillance of their communications.

timeline_en.title_en: Restricted internet access under total state control
timeline_en.description_en: Cuba allows internet access only at a few selected sites (hotels, state institutions). ETECSA, the state monopoly provider, controls the entire infrastructure. Huawei supplies network equipment. Access for ordinary citizens is extremely expensive and limited. All internet access passes through state-controlled nodes.

timeline_en.title_en: Introduction of mobile internet with built-in surveillance
timeline_en.description_en: Cuba introduces mobile internet for the first time, immediately under ETECSA control. Technical analyses show deep packet inspection (DPI) for content filtering. The infrastructure allows targeted blocking of individual services such as social media. VPN services are blocked during political events. Freedom House consistently rates Cuba as 'Not Free.'

timeline_en.title_en: #11J: largest protests in decades — internet fully shut down
timeline_en.description_en: On July 11, 2021, the largest anti-government protests in decades break out. Shortly after they begin, the Cuban government fully shuts down mobile internet. NetBlocks and Access Now document the shutdown in real time. Social media and messaging apps are blocked. Hundreds of demonstrators are arrested, many of whom report surveillance of their communications.

timeline_en.title_en: Rising surveillance capacities despite economic crisis
timeline_en.description_en: Despite a severe economic crisis, Cuba continues to invest in surveillance infrastructure. Freedom House reports increasingly targeted online repression. Journalists and opposition figures are convicted on the basis of their online activity. International attempts to enable free internet access (e.g. through Starlink authorizations) are blocked by the government.

sources_titles_en: Freedom on the Net 2021: Cuba
Freedom on the Net 2023: Cuba
Keep It On: Internet shutdowns in Cuba

laos-chinese-surveillance-export.json.name_en: Laos: Import of Chinese Surveillance Systems — Safe City and Facial Recognition
laos-chinese-surveillance-export.json.description_en: Laos has imported Chinese surveillance technology from Huawei and ZTE as part of the Belt and Road Initiative, including Safe City systems with facial recognition, camera networks, and network surveillance infrastructure. The Carnegie Endowment AI Surveillance Index lists Laos among countries using Chinese AI surveillance exports for repressive purposes. ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights criticize the lack of contract transparency and democratic oversight.

timeline_en.title_en: Smart City MoU signed with China
timeline_en.description_en: As part of the Belt and Road Initiative, Laos signs several memoranda of understanding with Chinese technology companies to introduce smart city systems in Vientiane. Huawei and ZTE receive contracts to build surveillance camera networks, facial recognition systems, and 5G infrastructure. The contracts are not published.

timeline_en.title_en: Deployment of Safe City systems in Vientiane
timeline_en.description_en: Reports emerge about operational use of Safe City surveillance systems in the capital, Vientiane. Cameras with facial recognition capability are installed at intersections, government buildings, and public squares. The Interior Ministry announces use for crime fighting; independent verification is not possible.

timeline_en.title_en: Expansion to additional provinces and border crossings
timeline_en.description_en: Laos extends the Chinese surveillance infrastructure to border crossings and provincial cities. ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights warn that the system is being operated in one of Southeast Asia's most repressive states without any legal safeguards. Opposition figures and ethnic minorities, in particular Hmong communities, are potential targets.

timeline_en.title_en: International criticism without consequence — Laos remains a one-party state
timeline_en.description_en: Laos ranks as 'Not Free' in the Freedom House report and shows no signs of democratic reform. The surveillance infrastructure consolidates LPRP (Lao People's Revolutionary Party) control. Human rights reports document increasing self-censorship among the population. The international community responds with few concrete measures to the technology transfer.

sources_titles_en: The Global Expansion of AI Surveillance
Freedom in the World 2023: Laos

nso-pegasus-spyware.json.description_en: The Israeli company NSO Group sells the AI-assisted surveillance software Pegasus to governments worldwide. The program uses zero-day exploits to fully take over smartphones and is deployed against journalists, human rights defenders, and opposition figures. The Pegasus Project exposed the global dimension of the abuse in 2021.
actors_en: Various governments (Saudi Arabia, Morocco, Hungary, among others)

timeline_en.title_en: First Pegasus infections documented
timeline_en.description_en: Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto documents the first Pegasus infections on the iPhone of human rights activist Ahmed Mansoor in the UAE. The software exploits three zero-day vulnerabilities (Trident) to fully take over the device.

timeline_en.title_en: WhatsApp lawsuit against NSO Group
timeline_en.description_en: WhatsApp/Meta sues NSO Group in a US federal court for exploiting a vulnerability in WhatsApp through which Pegasus was installed on the devices of roughly 1,400 users, including journalists and activists.

timeline_en.title_en: Pegasus Project: global exposure
timeline_en.description_en: A consortium of 17 media organizations coordinated by Forbidden Stories publishes the Pegasus Project investigation. A leaked list of more than 50,000 phone numbers reveals the scale of global surveillance: journalists, opposition figures, lawyers, and heads of state in more than 40 countries are affected.

timeline_en.title_en: US adds NSO Group to sanctions list
timeline_en.description_en: The US Commerce Department adds NSO Group to the Entity List. Apple sues NSO Group and introduces security updates (Lockdown Mode). The European Parliament sets up an inquiry committee (PEGA).

timeline_en.title_en: WhatsApp wins against NSO Group
timeline_en.description_en: A US federal judge rules in favor of WhatsApp/Meta in the case against NSO Group. The court finds that NSO violated the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. The ruling creates an important precedent for spyware vendor liability.

sources_titles_en: The Million Dollar Dissident: NSO Group's iPhone Zero-Days
Pegasus Project: Global Abuse of Surveillance Technology Exposed
EU Parliament: PEGA Committee Investigation Report

oesterreich-ki-ams-algorithmus.json.name_en: Austria: AMS Algorithm Discriminates Against Women and Older Jobseekers
oesterreich-ki-ams-algorithmus.json.description_en: Austria's Public Employment Service (AMS) developed an algorithmic system starting in 2018 to sort jobseekers into three opportunity categories. The system reproduced structural discrimination patterns: women, people over 50, and people with disabilities were assigned to lower categories, leading to fewer resources and support measures. After public pressure, a critical opinion from the data protection authority, and a lawsuit, the planned full rollout was postponed and ultimately reassessed.

timeline_en.title_en: Development of the AMS scoring algorithm
timeline_en.description_en: AMS commissions the development of a machine learning system to automatically classify jobseekers into three opportunity categories: high chances (group A), medium chances (group B), and low chances (group C). The categorization is meant to steer the allocation of counseling resources and support measures. Critics point out from the start that historical employment data inscribes structural inequalities into the system.

timeline_en.title_en: Planned rollout sparks public debate
timeline_en.description_en: When the planned rollout of the algorithm becomes known, women's rights organizations, unions, and NGOs sharply criticize the system. Analyses show that the model systematically rates women worse than comparable men — solely on the basis of gender as a variable — and that older and disabled jobseekers are structurally disadvantaged.

timeline_en.title_en: Data protection authority rebukes the algorithmic system
timeline_en.description_en: The Austrian Data Protection Authority (DSB) finds in a report that the AMS algorithm violates data protection law because it does not provide the required transparency and explainability. The authority demands corrections. AMS suspends full operation of the algorithm and runs it only in the background, with no direct effect on funding decisions.

timeline_en.title_en: Judicial and political review
timeline_en.description_en: Data protection organizations file formal complaints; courts confirm fundamental legal concerns about the system's use. The Austrian parliament debates regulation of algorithmic decision-making systems in the public sector. The case becomes a reference point in the EU AI Act debate on high-risk AI systems in employment.

sources_titles_en: Austria: Dispute over the AMS algorithm enters the next round
Data protection officials: AMS algorithm must be shut down immediately
Can algorithms discriminate?
AMS algorithm: points deducted for women, mothers, and over-50s

pakistan-ki-blasphemie-ueberwachung.json.name_en: Pakistan: AI Surveillance to Enforce Blasphemy Laws
pakistan-ki-blasphemie-ueberwachung.json.description_en: Pakistan deploys AI-assisted social media surveillance to identify 'blasphemous' online content. The Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) uses automated monitoring tools to scan social media posts. Blasphemy can be punished by death in Pakistan. Hundreds of people are arrested for online statements, and several have been killed by mobs after blasphemy accusations.

timeline_en.title_en: PECA: law criminalizing online blasphemy
timeline_en.description_en: Pakistan passes the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), which criminalizes 'blasphemy' on the internet. The FIA receives powers for digital surveillance and sets up a cybercrime unit that automatically scans social media posts for 'blasphemous' content.

timeline_en.title_en: Death penalty for a Facebook post
timeline_en.description_en: Taimoor Raza is sentenced to death over a Facebook post — the first death sentence worldwide for a social media post. The case shows the lethal convergence of automated surveillance and draconian blasphemy laws. At least four other people are sentenced to death for online blasphemy.

timeline_en.title_en: Escalation: automated removal and lynchings
timeline_en.description_en: Pakistan compels social media platforms to install filtering systems and automated reporting channels. In parallel, at least 80 people are attacked or killed by mobs over blasphemy accusations — often triggered by viral social media posts. Algorithms that flag content as 'blasphemous' become tools of vigilante justice.

timeline_en.title_en: International criticism and flight
timeline_en.description_en: UNHCR reports rising asylum applications from Pakistanis accused of blasphemy. The EU and UN special rapporteurs call for the abolition of the blasphemy laws. Pakistan instead tightens surveillance and threatens social media platforms with shutdowns. The use of AI to enforce religious laws becomes a global precedent.

sources_titles_en: Pakistan's Blasphemy Law Targets Youth on Social Media
Pakistan Submission to the UN Human Rights Committee
Pakistan blasphemy accusations: Islamist gang entraps, extorts
TikToker held on blasphemy charges in Muzaffargarh
World Report 2025: Pakistan

pakistan-safe-city-lahore.json.name_en: Pakistan: Safe City Project Lahore and Islamabad — Chinese Surveillance Technology for Mass Control
pakistan-safe-city-lahore.json.description_en: Pakistan has built comprehensive Safe City systems in Lahore and Islamabad using Chinese technology, connecting thousands of surveillance cameras with facial recognition, automatic license plate recognition, and centralized data storage. The Punjab Safe Cities Authority (PSCA) system in Lahore is considered one of the largest in South Asia. Civil liberties groups and investigative media document concerns about political surveillance, the absence of data protection laws, and use against demonstrators.
actors_en: Pakistani government / Punjab Safe Cities Authority (PSCA)

timeline_en.title_en: Inauguration of the Safe City system in Islamabad
timeline_en.description_en: Pakistan inaugurates the first Safe City system in Islamabad using Chinese technology. The system comprises over 1,900 surveillance cameras connected to a central control center. The infrastructure is financed under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) and is part of broader digital cooperation between the two states.

timeline_en.title_en: Expansion of the Lahore system by the Punjab Safe Cities Authority
timeline_en.description_en: The Punjab Safe Cities Authority expands the Lahore system to more than 8,000 cameras across the city. The PSCA receives broad powers to store and analyze data without adequate parliamentary oversight. Privacy International documents that Pakistan lacks a comprehensive data protection law to regulate the system's use.

timeline_en.title_en: Political surveillance concerns and misuse allegations
timeline_en.description_en: Investigative journalists at Dawn newspaper and international observers report that the Safe City system is being used during protests against the government to identify and track demonstrators. The facial recognition database is linked to biometric data from the national ID database without legal basis. Activists report intimidation after participating in protest events.

timeline_en.title_en: Calls for data protection law and parliamentary criticism
timeline_en.description_en: Pakistani civil liberties groups and international NGOs call for a comprehensive data protection law. Parliament debates a Personal Data Protection Bill that falls short of international standards on key points. The Safe City system continues to expand to additional cities, including Karachi and Peshawar.

sources_titles_en: Safe City Project launched in Islamabad
PSCA surveillance network and civil liberties concerns

palantir-ice-ueberwachung.json.name_en: Palantir & ICE: AI-Assisted Immigration Surveillance in the US
palantir-ice-ueberwachung.json.description_en: US immigration agency ICE uses Palantir's FALCON data analysis platform to aggregate personal data on immigrants en masse and plan deportation operations. The system links databases from law enforcement, social benefits, driver's licenses, and social media to identify people without legal status — including in so-called 'sanctuary cities.'

timeline_en.title_en: Palantir-ICE contract for FALCON system
timeline_en.description_en: ICE signs contracts with Palantir Technologies for the FALCON platform (later known as ICM — Investigative Case Management). The system enables the linking of data from more than 1,200 sources, including DMV driver records, utility bills, school registrations, and social media profiles.

timeline_en.title_en: Trump administration escalates deportations
timeline_en.description_en: Under the Trump administration, Palantir's tools are aggressively deployed to expand deportation operations. ICE agents use FALCON to track down people who came into contact with authorities only over traffic violations or as witnesses. The ACLU documents cases in which parents are identified during their children's school enrollment.

timeline_en.title_en: Palantir's role in family separations exposed
timeline_en.description_en: Investigative reports and leaked documents show that Palantir's systems were used in organizing the family separation policy at the US-Mexico border. More than 5,000 children are separated from their parents. Palantir employees protest internally against the ICE contract.

timeline_en.title_en: Growing resistance and transparency reports
timeline_en.description_en: The Mijente report 'Who's Behind ICE?' documents the full technology supply chain of the deportation machinery. Several US cities pass anti-surveillance ordinances. Georgetown Law's Center on Privacy & Technology publishes 'American Dragnet,' revealing the dimensions of DHS surveillance infrastructure.

sources_titles_en: Palantir Provides the Engine for Donald Trump's Deportation Machine
American Dragnet: Data-Driven Deportation in the 21st Century

peru-ki-protest-ueberwachung.json.name_en: Peru: Surveillance Technology Against Protesters After the 2022 State Crisis
peru-ki-protest-ueberwachung.json.description_en: After the impeachment and arrest of President Pedro Castillo in December 2022 and the subsequent mass protests — particularly in the Andean regions — the Peruvian state deployed surveillance technology to identify and pursue demonstrators. Human Rights Watch documented the use of cameras and databases to identify protesters who were then arrested. The EFF flagged the use of social media surveillance tools. Indigenous communities and citizens from poorer Andean regions, who were the main drivers of the protest movement, were particularly affected.

timeline_en.title_en: Political crisis and mass protests — mobilization of the surveillance apparatus
timeline_en.description_en: After President Castillo's failed self-coup and arrest, Peru is plunged into a serious political crisis. Tens of thousands of protesters, mostly from indigenous communities in Cusco, Puno, and other Andean regions, travel to Lima and block roads and airports. The government declares a state of emergency and activates security infrastructure including Lima's camera networks.

timeline_en.title_en: Violent crackdown with documented surveillance tools
timeline_en.description_en: Human Rights Watch documents that during the violent dispersal of protests in Lima, Ayacucho, and other cities, security forces specifically arrest people who had previously been identified on surveillance cameras. In protests in Juliaca, 18 people are killed. The EFF flags the use of commercial social media surveillance platforms by Peruvian authorities without any legal basis.

timeline_en.title_en: Expansion of digital surveillance capacities without legal framework
timeline_en.description_en: Peruvian civil liberties groups and the EFF report that in the wake of the protests, authorities expand digital surveillance to map activist networks. Arrested demonstrators report that investigators demonstrated knowledge of their digital communications and movement profiles. A data protection law exists but is not applied to state surveillance. Indigenous activists report targeted tracking.

timeline_en.title_en: Impunity and ongoing threat to activists
timeline_en.description_en: No Peruvian security official is held accountable for the use of surveillance to suppress the protests. Human Rights Watch documents that several activists remain under observation and face threats. The UN Human Rights Council expresses concern about Peru's handling of protesters. Data protection authorities open no investigations into illegal surveillance.

sources_titles_en: Peru: Killings and injuries in protests could implicate president and chain of command as criminally responsible
Peruvian protests (2022-2023)
Peru: Dina Boluarte ordered the murder of protesters and must stand trial for crimes against humanity
Peru: Justice for Indigenous Protestors Killed by Police

philippinen-duterte-social-media-ki.json.name_en: Philippines: AI-Assisted Troll Armies and the Drug War
philippinen-duterte-social-media-ki.json.description_en: During the 'drug war' under President Duterte, AI-assisted social media manipulation campaigns were used to legitimize the systematic killing of more than 12,000 people. Coordinated bot networks and troll farms spread disinformation on Facebook — the dominant platform in the Philippines. Journalists such as Maria Ressa (2021 Nobel laureate) were targeted by orchestrated online campaigns.
actors_en: Duterte administration / Office of the President

timeline_en.title_en: Social media campaign and troll army
timeline_en.description_en: Duterte wins the presidential election with the help of a massive social media campaign. Investigations show a network of paid troll farms coordinating propaganda and overwhelming critics with shitstorms. Facebook is the primary information source for 97% of Filipino internet users.

timeline_en.title_en: Drug war and disinformation
timeline_en.description_en: Duterte's 'drug war' claims more than 6,000 lives according to official figures, more than 12,000 according to human rights groups. Social media campaigns portray victims as criminals and delegitimize criticism. Automated accounts spread false information about human rights organizations and independent media.

timeline_en.title_en: Facebook removes coordinated networks
timeline_en.description_en: Facebook removes coordinated Filipino fake-account networks linked to the military for the first time. The removed pages and groups had millions of followers. Rappler editor Maria Ressa documents that she receives an average of 90 hate messages per hour — many from bots and coordinated accounts.

timeline_en.title_en: Nobel Prize for Ressa and international attention
timeline_en.description_en: Maria Ressa receives the Nobel Peace Prize together with Dmitry Muratov 'for their fight for freedom of expression.' The ICC opens preliminary investigations into the drug war. Facebook/Meta acknowledges content moderation failures. The case becomes a global reference point for the role of social media in legitimizing state violence.

sources_titles_en: Propaganda War: Weaponizing the Internet
Philippines: War on Drugs
Maria Ressa - Facts - Nobel Peace Prize 2021
Removing Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior from the Philippines

philippinen-ki-red-tagging.json.name_en: Philippines: Algorithmic Red-Tagging of Activists Leads to Killings
philippinen-ki-red-tagging.json.description_en: The Philippine military and the government agency NTF-ELCAC use social media analysis and databases to label activists, journalists, lawyers, and left-wing politicians as communist sympathizers ('red-tagging'). This digital marking is demonstrably linked to extrajudicial killings: people on the lists are killed or 'disappeared.' The UN and Human Rights Watch document hundreds of cases.
actors_en: NTF-ELCAC (National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict)

timeline_en.title_en: Founding of NTF-ELCAC and build-up of databases
timeline_en.description_en: President Duterte establishes NTF-ELCAC by executive order to coordinate all branches of the state to fight left-wing groups. At the same time, the systematic build-up of databases begins, classifying people as NPA sympathizers (communist guerrillas). Social media activity, union memberships, and NGO ties are analyzed.

timeline_en.title_en: Anti-Terror Law legalizes expanded surveillance
timeline_en.description_en: The Anti-Terror Law (Republic Act 11479) takes effect, giving authorities broad powers for surveillance and arrest without judicial authorization. Red-tagging lists are publicly spread in media and on social media to stigmatize those affected. More than 800 people are listed on official lists without a hearing.

timeline_en.title_en: 'Bloody Sunday': coordinated raids based on lists
timeline_en.description_en: On March 7, 2021, coordinated police raids ('Bloody Sunday') kill nine people who were on red-tagging lists. UN special rapporteurs condemn the killings as extrajudicial. Karapatan documents that since 2016 more than 400 activists who had been red-tagged have been killed. No prosecution of those responsible.

timeline_en.title_en: Practice continues under Marcos
timeline_en.description_en: Under the new president, Marcos Jr., red-tagging continues. An ICC preliminary investigation into Philippine crimes is underway, but the Philippines previously withdrew from the Rome Statute. Civil society and church representatives continue to be persecuted. Digital tools are normalized as legal surveillance. International criticism has so far brought no structural changes.

sources_titles_en: World Report 2024: Philippines

polen-ki-sozialleistungen-profiling.json.name_en: Poland: Algorithmic Profiling in the Welfare System Discriminates Against the Unemployed
polen-ki-sozialleistungen-profiling.json.description_en: Poland's employment agencies have used an algorithmic profiling system since 2014 that sorts unemployed people into three categories: 'favored,' 'average,' and 'not favored.' The algorithm assesses age, gender, disability status, and place of residence. People in rural areas and older residents systematically receive less support as a result. The Panoptykon Foundation and the Helsinki Committee criticize the system as discriminatory and opaque.
actors_en: Polish Ministry of Family and Social Policy

timeline_en.title_en: Introduction of the three-category profiling system
timeline_en.description_en: The Polish labor ministry introduces an algorithmic system that sorts unemployed people into three categories. Variables such as age, gender, disability, place of residence, and education level feed into the score. People classified as 'not favored' receive reduced support measures.

timeline_en.title_en: Panoptykon Foundation documents discriminatory effect
timeline_en.description_en: The Polish Panoptykon Foundation publishes an investigation showing that rural populations and older jobseekers are systematically rated worse. The algorithm perpetuates structural inequalities instead of countering them. GDPR concerns about automated decision-making are raised.

timeline_en.title_en: Lawsuit before the Constitutional Tribunal
timeline_en.description_en: The Helsinki Committee for Human Rights in Poland supports those affected with legal complaints against the profiling system. The Constitutional Tribunal opens a review. Initial expert opinions find that the system may violate Article 22 of the GDPR (automated decisions).

timeline_en.title_en: Partial reform under GDPR pressure
timeline_en.description_en: Poland modifies the system under pressure from the GDPR and initial court rulings. Those affected now have the right to request a human review of their classification. Full transparency about the weighting of the algorithm's variables is not, however, established. Human rights organizations call the reform inadequate.

sources_titles_en: Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights Poland — Social benefits and algorithmics

polen-pegasus-opposition.json.name_en: Poland: Pegasus Spyware Against Opposition Politicians
polen-pegasus-opposition.json.description_en: The Polish PiS government used NSO's Pegasus spyware to surveil opposition politicians, lawyers, and a prosecutor during the 2019 election campaign. The most prominent case is Senator Krzysztof Brejza, whose phone was hacked 33 times. Stolen messages were manipulated and broadcast on state television TVP to discredit the opposition.
actors_en: CBA (Centralne Biuro Antykorupcyjne / Central Anti-Corruption Bureau)

timeline_en.title_en: Pegasus deployed against opposition politicians during the campaign
timeline_en.description_en: During the 2019 parliamentary election campaign, the phone of Senator Krzysztof Brejza, the opposition's campaign manager, is infected with Pegasus at least 33 times. Lawyer Roman Giertych and prosecutor Ewa Wrzosek are also surveilled. Manipulated messages from Brejza's phone appear on the state news broadcast Wiadomosci.

timeline_en.title_en: Citizen Lab and AP confirm Pegasus infection
timeline_en.description_en: Citizen Lab forensically confirms the Pegasus infection on Brejza's phone. The Associated Press reports on the case. The PiS government initially denies its use before PiS leader Kaczynski confirms in an interview that Poland owns Pegasus, but claims it was used legally.

timeline_en.title_en: Senate inquiry committee
timeline_en.description_en: The Polish Senate sets up an inquiry committee. The European Parliament's PEGA committee travels to Warsaw. The ECtHR issues interim measures to protect the victims. Experts argue that the surveillance may have influenced the 2019 election outcome — PiS won by a narrow majority.

timeline_en.title_en: New government: investigation and reckoning
timeline_en.description_en: The new government under PM Tusk launches a comprehensive investigation into the use of Pegasus. A parliamentary inquiry committee is set up. The first charges of abuse of office are prepared. The case becomes a symbol of the misuse of surveillance technology in EU democracies.

sources_titles_en: EU Parliament: PEGA Committee Final Report

predpol-predictive-policing.json.description_en: The predictive policing algorithm PredPol (later renamed Geolitica) systematically reinforces racist policing in US cities. The system predicts where crimes will occur but is based on historical police data that reproduces and amplifies existing discrimination patterns.
affectedRights_en: right to fair treatment by law enforcement

timeline_en.title_en: PredPol developed and founded
timeline_en.description_en: PredPol is founded as a spin-off of academic research at UCLA. The algorithm is based on seismological models applied to crime data to predict hotspots.

timeline_en.title_en: LAPD adopts PredPol
timeline_en.description_en: The Los Angeles Police Department becomes one of the first major users of PredPol. The system is deployed in several police districts and determines which areas receive heightened patrolling.

timeline_en.title_en: Studies document racial bias
timeline_en.description_en: Several independent studies show that PredPol systematically marks predominantly Black and Latino neighborhoods as high-risk zones. The feedback loop reinforces existing policing patterns: more patrolling leads to more arrests, which generates more data that justifies more patrolling.

timeline_en.title_en: LAPD ends use of PredPol
timeline_en.description_en: After sustained criticism and the Black Lives Matter protests, the LAPD ends its use of PredPol. Several other police agencies follow suit and discontinue their use of predictive policing software.

timeline_en.title_en: PredPol rebrands as Geolitica
timeline_en.description_en: Under public pressure, PredPol rebrands as Geolitica. Despite the name change, the underlying algorithmic problems remain. The company finally ceases operations in 2023.

sources_titles_en: Crime Prediction Software Promised to Be Free of Biases. New Data Shows It Perpetuates Them.
LAPD ends predictive policing program

Data-Driven Policing: Campaign against algorithmic surveillance

ruanda-ki-smart-city.json.name_en: Rwanda: Smart City Surveillance Infrastructure and Authoritarian Use
ruanda-ki-smart-city.json.description_en: Since 2015, Rwanda has been building a comprehensive smart city and surveillance infrastructure in Kigali with the support of Chinese technology companies. The 'Kigali Safe City' project includes a nationwide network of surveillance cameras with facial recognition capability. While the government presents the system as a tool for public safety and economic development, human rights organizations warn of its use against opposition figures, journalists, and dissidents. Reports of Rwanda's transnational repression show that state surveillance operates beyond the country's borders.

timeline_en.title_en: Smart City initiatives and Chinese technology partnerships
timeline_en.description_en: Rwanda launches ambitious smart city programs as part of its Vision 2020 development strategy. Partnerships with Chinese companies are formed to build digital infrastructure, surveillance cameras, and broadband networks. The country presents itself as Africa's technology showcase. Privacy International and other organizations begin to document the dual character of the infrastructure for development and control.

timeline_en.title_en: Kigali Safe City: cameras, facial recognition, and AI analysis
timeline_en.description_en: The 'Kigali Safe City' project is officially launched. Hundreds of cameras are installed in the capital. Reports by The Guardian and Privacy International show that the system includes facial recognition capabilities. Human rights organizations point to Rwanda's documented history of persecuting opposition figures and journalists and warn of the misuse potential of the infrastructure.

timeline_en.title_en: COVID surveillance and expansion of the control infrastructure
timeline_en.description_en: Rwanda uses the COVID-19 pandemic to significantly expand surveillance measures. Drones with loudspeakers and cameras are deployed to enforce curfews. Contact-tracing systems are linked to existing surveillance databases. Critics note that the built-up capacities go far beyond pandemic-related needs.

timeline_en.title_en: Cross-border surveillance of Rwandan dissidents
timeline_en.description_en: The Guardian and Citizen Lab report cases in which Rwandan surveillance operations target dissidents and opposition politicians abroad, including in Europe and North America. Exiled journalists and opposition members report intimidation attempts and digital surveillance of their communications. The smart city infrastructure proves to be part of a broader system of political control.

rumaenien-wahlannullierung-tiktok.json.name_en: Romania: 2024 Presidential Election Annulled Over TikTok Algorithm Manipulation
rumaenien-wahlannullierung-tiktok.json.description_en: On December 6, 2024, Romania's Constitutional Court annulled the first round of the November 24, 2024 presidential election after declassified intelligence documents revealed a coordinated influence campaign on TikTok. Ultranationalist outsider Calin Georgescu had unexpectedly emerged as the winner of the first round, backed by more than 25,000 TikTok accounts and 5,000 Telegram channels that algorithmically amplified his messages. Russia is named as the suspected initiator of the hybrid campaign. It is the first time in EU history that a national election was annulled over algorithm manipulation on a social media platform.

timeline_en.title_en: Coordinated TikTok campaign builds reach
timeline_en.description_en: In the weeks before the first round, more than 25,000 TikTok accounts and 5,000 Telegram channels become active, coordinating content in favor of Calin Georgescu. The accounts amplify hashtags, generate engagement spikes, and manipulate the TikTok recommendation algorithm. Georgescu had polled below 5 percent before election day — a sudden visibility cascade on TikTok changed the picture dramatically.

timeline_en.title_en: First round: Georgescu surprisingly leads with around 22.9 percent
timeline_en.description_en: Calin Georgescu, a previously largely unknown ultranationalist candidate with a pro-Russian foreign policy, unexpectedly wins the first round ahead of all established candidates. Election observers and political analysts express surprise; several analyses attribute the success to TikTok reach. Second place goes to liberal Elena Lasconi.

timeline_en.title_en: President Iohannis declassifies intelligence reports
timeline_en.description_en: Outgoing President Klaus Iohannis releases declassified reports from the Romanian intelligence service SRI. The documents establish more than 34 documented hybrid operations by Russia against Romania in 2024, coordinated account clusters, algorithmic amplification, and paid promotion in favor of Georgescu. TikTok confirms it removed two account clusters (78 + 12 accounts) linked to Georgescu/Geoana.

timeline_en.title_en: Constitutional Court annuls the election — first EU precedent
timeline_en.description_en: The Romanian Constitutional Court unanimously annuls the first round and orders a full rerun. Georgescu speaks of an 'officially formalized coup.' The EU Commission opens formal DSA proceedings against TikTok. The 2025 election rerun is seen as the first major stress test of the EU Digital Services Act and of European democracies' resilience to algorithmic manipulation.

russland-gesichtserkennung-moskau.json.name_en: Russia: Facial Recognition in Moscow to Identify Demonstrators
russland-gesichtserkennung-moskau.json.description_en: Moscow operates one of the world's densest urban facial recognition networks with more than 100,000 cameras. The system, supplied by NtechLab, has been used for law enforcement since 2017 and deployed specifically against political demonstrators. During the 2021 protests in support of Alexei Navalny and following Russia's 2022 attack on Ukraine, numerous people were identified from camera footage and arrested. Civil liberties organizations document systematic misuse of the system for political repression.
actors_en: Moscow city government / Russian federal government

timeline_en.title_en: Introduction of the citywide facial recognition system
timeline_en.description_en: Moscow signs a contract with NtechLab and integrates facial recognition software into the city's existing camera network. NtechLab became known in 2015 through its 'FindFace' service, which could identify faces in social networks. The system is initially officially justified as a crime-fighting tool. Human rights advocates immediately warn of the misuse potential.

timeline_en.title_en: Expansion during the COVID pandemic and new legal foundations
timeline_en.description_en: Under the cover of COVID-19 quarantine control, the system is massively expanded. New laws enable expanded official use of biometric data. The network now comprises more than 100,000 cameras across Moscow, including in subway stations and public squares. Data protection authorities criticize the lack of legal basis for the use.

timeline_en.title_en: Mass arrests at Navalny protests via facial recognition
timeline_en.description_en: After Alexei Navalny's arrest in January 2021, nationwide demonstrations break out. In Moscow, numerous protest participants are arrested at home days after the demonstrations — identified solely from camera footage and facial recognition data. OVD-Info documents dozens of such cases. After Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the pattern continues at anti-war protests.

timeline_en.title_en: International condemnation and growing self-censorship
timeline_en.description_en: Human Rights Watch and OVD-Info document the systematic use of facial recognition to suppress political opposition. Demonstrators in Russia begin to actively hide their faces or avoid protest events out of fear of subsequent identification. European authorities discuss export bans on facial recognition technology to Russia. The network remains fully operational.

sources_titles_en: Russia: Police target peaceful protesters identified using facial recognition technology
How the Russian state uses cameras against protesters
Kremlin Leaks: How Putin's Regime is Building AI Surveillance Operations

russland-ki-deepfake-ukraine-krieg.json.name_en: Russia: AI Deepfakes and Disinformation in the Ukraine War
russland-ki-deepfake-ukraine-krieg.json.description_en: Since the start of the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Russia has systematically deployed AI-generated deepfakes and automated disinformation campaigns. The high point was a fake video of President Zelensky in which he supposedly calls for surrender. Meta, the EU DisinfoLab, and the Digital Forensic Research Lab (DFRLab) document coordinated AI-assisted propaganda reaching millions of people in Ukraine and worldwide.

timeline_en.title_en: Start of the invasion and simultaneous information war
timeline_en.description_en: With the start of the military invasion, Russia launches a massive parallel information operation. State media, bot networks, and coordinated social media accounts spread narratives justifying the attack. AI tools for image and video manipulation are used for propaganda.

timeline_en.title_en: Deepfake video of President Zelensky
timeline_en.description_en: An AI-generated deepfake video goes viral, showing President Zelensky supposedly calling on Ukrainian soldiers to surrender. Meta, YouTube, and Twitter take the video down, but it reaches millions of users beforehand. Zelensky refutes the video in a live broadcast. The event is considered the first major deepfake use in an active war.

timeline_en.title_en: Systematic escalation of AI propaganda
timeline_en.description_en: Meta publishes Threat Intelligence Reports on coordinated inauthentic behavior originating in Russia. DFRLab documents the use of AI to mass-produce fake news websites imitating European media brands. The EU DisinfoLab identifies networks with thousands of AI-generated fake accounts.

timeline_en.title_en: International countermeasures and debate over AI regulation
timeline_en.description_en: The EU strengthens the mandate of the East StratCom Task Force and funds media literacy programs. NATO officially recognizes cognitive warfare as a threat vector. The use of deepfakes in the Ukraine war accelerates international discussions about labeling obligations for AI-generated content.
